idiom_name: narrowest-interface narrowing plus an RAII scope guard that drops OS credentials
implementation_notes: C++ adds no authority model, but it supplies two idioms that replace the classic rights-object structure. First, hand each collaborator the narrowest type that still does its job - an abstract base with only the operations it needs, a const reference, a std::span over the caller's buffer instead of the container - so the component cannot even name the authority it must not use. Second, scope the OS privileges a component needs with RAII, so the drop runs in a destructor on every exit path including exceptions, where a C-style call placed after the work would be skipped; std::unique_ptr with a custom deleter is the same mechanism applied to a privileged handle, because the handle and its authority die with the owner. The classic form (a policy object with an explicit permission set) is still justified when rights are runtime data assigned to several in-process subjects, but note that in-process restrictions are not a security boundary in C++ - a cast or a leaked reference bypasses them - so the enforcement remains the process identity or sandbox the code runs in.
pitfalls: In-process narrowing is advice, not enforcement: const_cast, reinterpret_cast and a leaked reference all bypass the interface, so never count a narrowed type as a security boundary - the process identity and the sandbox carry that.
A guard that raises privilege and restores it in a destructor still holds the privilege for its whole scope: do not keep it alive across untrusted input, and make sure the destructor cannot throw.

Ownership leaks authority: passing a raw pointer or reference hands over everything the owner can do, and a unique_ptr only releases its deleter's authority when the object is actually destroyed - long-lived caches and singletons extend privilege lifetimes by accident.
